article.plain_text:
The ABSURDITY of how REALITY is defined in THIS WORLD is that perhaps only through DRUG-INDUCED dreams can one's TRUEST EMOTIONS finally find expression, while the secrets of that reality remain safely buried within a "MIRRORED WORLD." Take, for example, a certain transgender girl: she was only fourteen or fifteen years old and subjected to extremely cruel and unfair treatment. She was forced to wear a boys’ school uniform and keep her hair cut short in a masculine style. She was not permitted to buy or wear the cute clothes she liked, nor was she allowed to own the dolls she loved. She would even be scolded and ordered to throw away something as small as a cute charm attached to her schoolbag.
 She felt that she was not truly living, but merely functioning like a robot, carrying out the commands imposed on her by her family, society, and school. She believed that during those years when she was forced to “live as a boy,” the person going through the motions of everyday life was not really her. It was nothing more than an empty shell, kept alive only in a biological sense. What drove her to LSD was a wish that was, in itself, painfully simple: she wanted—just once, even if only an illusion, even if for a fleeting moment, and even if she were the only person in the entire world to see it—to catch a glimpse of the “self in the mirror” she had always dreamed of.
 Even knowing that, once she was sober again, she would realize that the entire experience had been nothing more than a beautiful, fleeting dream, she still longed for the chance to experience, just once in her lifetime, what it felt like to be what she herself could finally recognize as a “REAL GIRL.” She wanted to look into a mirror and see herself wearing the princess dress of her dreams, with long pink hair cascading around her—much like the fairy-tale fantasies common to many cisgender girls during childhood. 

The tragedy was that she had been born into a body others recognized as male. For a very long time, she was forced to survive in this world under a male identity. 

This compels us to seriously confront a question about the nature of perception and reality: after TAKING A HALLUCINOGEN, the self she EXPERIENCED AND SAW IN THE MIRROR—THE SELF WHO TRULY CORRESPONDED to her INNERMOST IDENTITY—could that self, in some sense, be more “REAL” than the “version” of her that lived her everyday life, moving through the world almost like the LIVING DEAD? 

WE
 DO
 NOT
 KNOW. 

Perhaps we will NEVER—NEVER—KNOW.
 Ultimately, we know only this: after the effects of the drug wore off and she returned to the “NORMAL WORLD,” the girl in the mirror—the “REAL” her from the dream world—“DISAPPEARED.” The beauty that should have been hers—the beauty she should have been allowed to express, the endearing charm she should have been free to radiate, and the happiness she deserved—all became like FIREWORKS BLOOMING ALONE IN THE NIGHT SKY, WITH NO ONE THERE TO WATCH: fleeting, unnoticed, ignored, and understood by no one.
 And even THAT had to be brought into existence THROUGH CHEMICALS.
